Would it not be better to encourage Canadian manufacturers by having their goods carried to the people of British Columbia, even if the steamers do call at New York instead of Montreal or St. John in the meantime, or until we can make the necessary arrangements to have a line of steamships from St. John to Vancouver? Now, I want to continue this article from the Sun:
The distance from Vancouver to Halifax is 1,450 miles greater than from Vancouver to New York.
That should be that the distance from Vancouver to Montreal is 1,450 miles greater than from Vancouver to New York.
1.	To the eastern Canadian manufacturers- By their thus being able to ship their products ''in bond1' to British Columbia-thence to Russia, Japan, China, New Zealand and Australia-at the minimum rates, in competition with the manufactured goods from Europe or the United States.
2.	To the manufacturers and producers of British Columbia, as it will provide lowest cost of transportation "inwards" for raw materials, as Well as lowest rates for export of products "outwards."
3.	To the consumers of British Columbia, and to those of western Canada up by rail through British Columbia, in getting a fairer ratio of prices for all commodities.
4.	To the ports of Vancouver, Victoria, New Westminster and Prince Rupert, by encouraging shipping, especially from Britain, to call at New York for Canadian (goods' for British Columbia, the Orient, and vice versa.
The only thing which prevents us from profiting by the offer of the Maple Leaf Line is a letter from the Minister of Customs to the Customs Department at tips port prohibiting the admission of Canadian goods arriving by sea if they have passed by the short haul over United States rails to such ports as Boston and New York.
You see, if that is a correct statement, the Minister of Customs is prohibiting the

entry of such goods into the ports of British Columbia.
It is not necessary to amend a statute or repeal an order in council. It has never been pretended that the action of the Minister of Customs was dictated by the Government as a matter of policy. Beyond their apparent reluctance to order a withdrawal of the letter, there is nothing to show that British Columbia's unfortunate position is due to anything but the personal act of the Hon. J. D. Reid, dictated by the manufacturers of Ontario or eastern railway interests, and both these interests, we submit, have acted on a narrow and mistaken view as to the results which would follow from allowing British Columbia to enjoy the use of the great advantages supplied by nature.
From the correspondence that I have received I believe that neither the railways nor the Manufacturers' Association are particularly opposed to this.

That man is off about
the manufacturers being opposed to it because they want to get their goods in the cheapest way they can.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. REID (Minister of Customs):
speechtext:
This matter has been before me for some little time, as has been stated by the hon. member for Assiniboia, and it has given me great concern. I personally am anxious to do all I can for the province of British Columbia or any other part of the Dominion. I must say that my hon. friend treats this question very lightly. All we have to do, he says, is to put an officer
in New York and the whole matter is settled. He tells us that American officers are at Vancouver for the purpose of seeing that American goods are sent through from there to the United States. That may be true. But let me explain the bonding privileges between Canada' and the United States. The bonding privileges allow a car that is loaded with goods and sealed at Vancouver to be shipped through to its destination and the seal broken by the officers of the same country. In the case mentioned by my hon. friend, the fish caught Sn American waters up at Alaska, and brought down to Vancouver, have to be transported as quickly as possible. The American officers see the fish loaded on to the cars, the American seal is put on the car, and when the car gets to New York the seal is broken by an American officer; so the car is both sealed and unsealed by American officers. Similarly, if a manufacturer ineastern Canada wants .to route through the-United States some goods he is shipping to British Columbia or some place in the-West, the car is sealed by a Canadian; officer before it leaves Canada; it them passes through the United States, comes-in,to Canada again, and the seal is broken at the car's destination by a Canadian officor. My hon. friend can see that there is therefore no possible chance of these goods being exchanged or getting out of the possession of Canadian Customs officers.
Mr. 1URRIFF: My hon. friend would not suggest that it would be impossible for a Canadian Customs officer in New York to see the goods transferred from the car to the steamship without being changed.

I was coming to that. The hon. member says that the Maple Leaf line is willing to pay for an officer, and he says that all these goods that are going to New York will be carried by a British line of steamers. The Maple Leaf Line is owned by the United States Steel Corporation, which is one of the largest corporations in the United States; and which, I believe from information I have received, is the one that is raising this agitation and is trying to prove to the people of British Columbia that they would gain great advantage if their line of steamers were to carry this freight from eastern Canada to-British Columbia. They have also used the argument that the goods would always be carried on British steamers. Now, we cannot control the port of New York or any

other American port. Would the hon. member advise us to put a customs officer in New York to see to it that goods shipped to a British Columbia port or elsewhere should not be carried by American steamers leaving for those ports, but must be carried on British steamers? Would not that be likely to cause trouble with the United States? Our relations are most friendly, and for us to absolutely refuse to allow our products to go out of an American port on an American vessel would be very likely to raise trouble.
They do not want you to confine yourself to British boats. But would it be possible to establish a customs office and have the shipping that way?

I was just coming to the
question of putting it on another vessel. I have stated that the bonding privileges must always apply to a Canadian or British vessel, for you could not ship in a foreign vessel and keep control. We, as British subjects, would have no control over that vessel.

Then, you cannot ship
in bond via New York to Vancouver?

It is a' very difficult matter
to arrange. I have found so many difficulties in it that I have not been able to carry out the wishes of those who have raised this agitation. Another question has come up. This House has always been of the opinion that, if possible, we should carry our goods through our own country.
We all agree with that.

When some of the people
from British Columbia were here to interview me on this matter, they led me to believe that the freights via New York were very much lower than they would be overland to Vancouver-that is, from such ports as Montreal, Toronto, or Hamilton.
By rail?

Yes. They said that the rate from New York to Vancouver would be, I think, 50c. per 100 lb. I asked the Chairman of the Railway Commission to instruct his officials to make out a statement showing the rates by rail on a long list of articles commonly shipped between eastern Canada and Vancouver. Then I had the officials put alongside these rates the rates from such places as Montreal, Toronto, and Hamilton, to New York, with the 50c. peT

100 lb. added as the freight to Vancouver. To these rates must be added insurance and wharfage charges, I find that there is very little difference between the charge on a full carload, shipped from eastern Canada by rail to Vancouver, and the same quantity shipped to New York and thence by vessel to Vancouver. Of course, all that I am saying now refers to rates under normal conditions, not rates charged under war conditions. The difference of these rates under normal conditions would be so small that I do not believe there is a member of the House who would ever discuss the matter if he had before nim the statement which I have had prepared. I also had a statement made out showing the local freights on smaller lots such as a ton or 500 lb. Of course, on these small lots and with local rates, the rates were very much higher by rail, and it would pay better to send by New York. But I do not consider it quite fair to make comparison with the local rates in this way. As to goods going in carload lots, there is very little ground of complaint when the whole matter is looked into. Besides, the only points to which these lower rates via New York would apply, would be Victoria and Vancouver. In inland places, like Kamloops for instance, the same would not apply.

But the minister will
find that the rail rate from Montreal to Kamloops, which is a couple of hundred miles east of Vancouver, is very much higher than the rate to Vancouver.

I was just about to say that. I suppose that it is on account of the water competition at coast points. There are two other reasons why I have had to give this matter most serious consideration before disposing of it.
We have built up in this country a great railway system between eastern and western Canada. The province of British Columbia has incurred large liabilities in connection with railways that have been built in that province. The Dominion Government itself is trying to develop the territory betwen here and British Columbia as well as to develop the Canadian Railway systems. The hon. member for Assiniboia advocates that instead of sending freight to British Columbia by our railway system we should send it to New York and thence by steamer through the Panama canal to Vancouver and Victoria. I think we

should consider carefully any proposed action which would tend to injure our railway system. Two years ago an agitation was started in British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba for the reduction of treight_ratee. It was shown on that occasion that if reduction were granted the railways would not be able to pay the expenses of operation, and that great injury would result to the West. No member of this House has been more strongly in favour of the development of our own great harbours than I have. I have been a party to assisting Vancouver and Victoria in their harbour development. I have also done what I could in the matter of the development of the ports of Montreal, Quebec, St. John and Halifax. If there is to be connection :by water through the Panama canal between eastern and western Canada, I believe that a line of steamships should be established leaving Montreal and Quebec in the summer and St. John and Halifax in the winter. I have asked persons with whom I have discussed this matter if some arrangement could be made by which the Maple Leaf line in the summer should come to Montreal and Quebec and in the winter to St. John and Halifax in order that our goods carried between the East and the West should go through our own Canadian ports. It is suggested that we put an officer in New York until the rwar is over or until we can arrange for the operation of this line. My experience, 'however, has been such as to lead me to believe that if you establish
a route	*by	putting an	officer at	a port	of	this- kind,	the	routewill remain	for all time	to	come.
If we should do that in this case, when we should come to arrange for the operation of a line of steamers leaving Montreal and Quebec in the summer and St. John and Halifax in the winter, we would be handicapped by that arrangement which we had made. It does not seem to me that the present is the proper time to bring this matter up. It is true that it is about two years since this agitation started. But it is nearly two years since war was declared between Great Britain and Germany and since that time it has been practically impossible to get vessels to carry the traffic between Canada and the Mother Country. I understand that at the present time the Maple Leaf Line have no sailings via the Panama canal; and my information is that you cannot count on any line of steamers doing this work at least until the war is over. Even
if steamers could be obtained to carry freight between New York, Seattle and Vancouver by the Panama canal, rates are so high owing to war conditions that there would be no- advantage in shipping by that route. I have given the reasons why I believe that this matter should remain in abeyance at least until the war is over. Having regard to the existing conditions, to the railway situation, to the intention of the Government to hold an investigation into railway matters with a view of reorganizing our railway system and to the policy of the Government in the matter of the development of our harbours-Montreal, Quebec, Halifax, St. John, Vancouver and Victoria-I feel that the committee will agree that the matter should rest until, a later date.

Under the permission which was given to the members by the Minister of Customs last night to bring up any subject when the House went into Supply to-day, I would like to bring to the attention of the minister and of the committee the case of an elector of the county of Missisquoi, one Albert Ernest Lagrange of Frelighsburg. On June 23, 1913, Mr. Lagrange, who is a cattle buyer, purchased from different farmers throughout his locality a car-load of hogs, which he loaded for shipment to Montreal. It was later ascertained by a very vigilant officer of the Department of Customs, Mr. Frank Fyles, of Abercorn, that there were in this carload three or four hogs which had been imported from the United States and on which no duty had been paid. These hogs were imported not by Mr. Lagrange, but by the party from whom he had purchased them. The entire car-load was held up and seized and in order to release the car from seizure, Mr. Lagrange followed it to St. Johns, the port of entry, and there placed in the hands of the collector of customs his cheque for $1,600, the full value of the carload of hogs. The hogs were released the next day and sent to Montreal. After having been sent to Montreal and disposed of, steps were taken to ascertain where the different hogs were purchased and it was discovered that four of these hogs had been smuggled in from the United States by a farmer called Peter Larose, of Frelighsburg. He was a tenant farmer and had no property except a team of horses, a very valuable wagon, and a set of harness. The outfit which he used to smuggle in the hogs was seized by an officer of the
/

department. Mr. Larose, however, happened to be a friend of the party in power, and' had voted for the defeated Conservative candidate in Missisquoi county. That defeated Conservative candidate came to the Tescue. After he had had an interview with some official in the Department of Customs at Ottawa this team of horses, the harness and wagon, which were worth $250 to $300, were released upon the payment of $50 to the department by Peter Larose. In the eyes of the department he had paid the penalty for having smuggled the hogs into Canada, This occurred in 1913, and we are now in the year of grace 1916, and the $1,000 deposited by this man LaGrange is still in the hands of the department, and the department absolutely refuses to refund this money to him. I have looked through the reports of the Auditor General and of the department, and I can find no entry showing to what purpose this money has been applied. I will go further. About a year after it had been proven that this man 'had had nothing to do with the smuggling in of the hogs which happened to be in his carload, he went to a Conservative member who occupies a seat on the other side of this House and gave him a synopsis of his case. I prefer not to mention this member's name publicly, but I can give it privately to the minister if he so desires. This Conservative member told the man he would have no difficulty whatever in getting the money, and he asked him to make a deposit of $25, which the Conservative member still has while the department still has the $1,600.
This matter was brought to my attention on April 24 of the present year, and naturally I took the step that any hon. member of Parliament would have taken in connection with the matter. I did not bother the minister, but went direct to the department and saw Mr. McDougald, the Commissioner of Customs. He reported that this matter had been pending for three years, and that no decision had yet been given by the minister. The matter was still pending when I saw the Commission-5 p m. er of Customs on April 28, 1916.
I asked him then if there was any reason why this deposit should be forfeited and he told me that he did not know as the matter was still in the hands of the minister, who was taking a very long time to make up his mind. I asked him to bring the matter to the attention of the minister at once and he promised to do so, and on May 1, 1916, he wrote me as follows:

Ottawa, May 1, 1916.
Geo. H. Boivin, Esq., M.P.,
House of Commons,
Ottawa.
Be Seizure No. 18860/89-A. E. LaGrange. Dear Sir,-Referring to your inquiry as to the above seizure, I am to state that the deposit of $1,600 is held as forfeited.
1 have the honour to he,
Sir,
Your obedient servant,
(Sgd.) John McDougald,
Commissioner.
He got off cheap; he oould have been prosecuted as well.

Remember that the charge was for smuggling in three or four hogs, that these hogs were in a oarload which was shipped to Montreal by am indirect route at a great loss to this man, that it was discovered that these hogs had been imported by somebody else, that the party who smuggled them in paid the penalty exacted by the department-and, after all this, the deposit is still held by the department. I am bringing this matter up in order to ascertain from the minister what I could not ascertain from the Commissioner of Customs, and that is, why the full value of the whole cargo of hogs was confiscated by the department when only three or four hogs had been smuggled into Canada by another party?

The hon. gentleman must
understand that hundreds of cases of this kind come before me, and each case is dealt with on its merits. In some cases we exact merely the value of the article seized, in other cases we impose a penalty as well, and in other cases we have prosecuted. In this particular case a seizure was made by our officers. I do not know whether my hon. friend knows this man, but my information is that he has been buying American hogs for many years all along the line, and shipping them to Montreal. This had a double effect. In the first place, the farmers living along the line where he was buying had to compete with American 'hogs that were smuggled in, and this man knew he was doing the farmers the greatest possible injury by bringing in American hogs and breaking the price on this side. The hon. member knows that drovers, when they are buying hogs or cattle, go right into a man's place and see the stock; they know whether that man has had those hogs before. The reason I made the man pay the full value of the carload was that I was of the opinion that lie knew well

enough those hogs had been smuggled in by this poor man; perhaps he wanted_ to benefit' by the lower price and got the poor man to smuggle them in. I had certain other information, and I do not believe the hon. member could get that man to make an affidavit that he did not know that those hogs had1 been smuggled in. According to my information he has been getting Ameri-^ can hogs in for years, thereby doing great' injury to our own Canadian farmers and to the treasury of Canada. Furthermore, although he knew that the Department of Agriculture had prohibited American hogs from coming into Canada, he had been bringing them in for years and taking chances of spreading hog cholera and other diseases amongst our Canadian stock. The hon. gentleman may think that the penalty was severe, but I can tell him that the man would not make an affidavit that this was the only case of smuggling in of hogs that he knew of. I think	he got	off very lightly.
I maintain that he got off very easily, and if he ever does the same again while I am minister, I want the hon. member to tell him that I will not only impose the penalty of a fine, but prosecute him as far as the law will allow.
The hon. minister seems to forget altogether that it was the other man who smuggled the hogs and was punished for doing so.
I will explain that. This man was a poor man who had nothing in the world but a team of horses.
He is a tenant farmer.

He was probably sent over by the other man to smuggle the hogs in. The hon. member says I should have treated this poor man as I treated the other man who is a wealthy man and has been smuggling in hogs for years and bringing disease into the country. He wants me to treat this poor unfortunate man who has nothing in the world but a team of horses the same as the other man who is wealthy, but I will not do that. The penalty I imposed on the man with the team of horses was a fine of $50, and to him that $50 was five times more of a penalty than it would be to a man who had a carload of hogs. I say that this poor tenant farmer was led into the difficulty by the other man, and I think that / the warning which the latter got was not only good for him but for all the people
in that district who may have been induced by him to do the same thing. I do not want, nor does this Government or any other government want to take the last dollar from a poor man. We want to give him a chance and a fair warning. With regard to the man who paid the $1,500, I want to say that if ever he gets into a scrape again he will not get so easily off.

I quite agree that a man who' is caught smuggling ought to pay the penalty. .1 think that everybody in this House agrees with that view, but I do not think that a man should be punished because the minister has heard through a third or fourth party that he may possibly have smuggled in years gone by. That is not the question before the House now, and it is not the question which should have been considered by the hon. minister, and the minister knows it. I will go further and say that if this man had been a good political supporter of the defeated Conservative candidate as Peter Larose is, he would have been treated differently. This man proved to the satisfaction of the department that every hog in that car had been purchased from a bona fide Canadian farmer who had got for it the bona fide Canadian price. Peter Larose was not merely a teamster who had nothing in the world 'but a team of horses and a wagon. He was a tenant farmer, residing upon the farm of Miss Chamberlain, at Frelighsburg, and the cheque which was given to him for the hogs was made payable to the order of the owner of the farm. It is impossible for the minister to say that one single hog in that car was smuggled with the knowledge of the man who put up the $1,600. The minister says that in years gone by this man had smuggled hogs from the United States. All I can say is that, if the minister has on that part of the line collectors of customs who will allow any man to smuggle in hogs for four years, and go unpunished, they should be dismissed, and officials should be appointed in their place who would do their duty and punish the smugglers. This man is willing to go before any court in the country and to pay any fine that may be imposed on him by any court in the country if he is found guilty, but having made in good faith a deposit with the collector of customs at St. Johns, which the collector promised would be returned to him in full if he established where the hogs came from, and having lost the interest

on the money for four years without receiving any communication from the minister and without being told of its confiscation, he objects to receiving a curt letter informing him that the deposit' is to be held, but without giving any reason for the minister's action. One thing the minister could at least do. This mail gave a Conservative member of Parliament $25 to use his influence on his behalf, and I would ask the minister to use his influence with the Conservative member of Parliament to have the money returned to Mr. La Grange. If the minister has any proof to offer against him, he should prosecute him, but I do object, and I think every fair-minded member in this House should object to the Minister of Customs constituting himself judge and jury in every case that comes before him, especially when he has no evidence before him but hearsay evidence that the man may have smuggled two or three years previously.

I have taken
some interest in the dijscussiton of (the Militia Estimates, and when they weTe under consideration on the last occasion it was arranged with the Prime Minister that an item should be left standing so that I might have the privilege of discussing a certain matter. I will not delay the House to any great length; I merely wish to express in a formal manner the opinion which I hold very strongly, and which I know is held by others, that the time has come when there should be a more liberal allowance to the dependents of soldiers who are serving. When the war broke out it was arranged that a separation allowance amounting I think to twenty dollars a month should be given to the families of soldiers who had enlisted. That is supplemented in some cases by assigned pay. It was agreed that the separation allowance and the assigned pay were not adequate support for the dependents under the existing conditions of the country, and so the Patriotic Fund was organized for the purpose of collecting money from the public at large to supplement the separation allowance and the assigned pay and so bring the measure of support available to the dependents of soldiers up to a point which, in the words of the Patriotic Fund circular, would provide a decent living.
Last year I took the view which I propose to express at the present time, namely,

that while the Patriotic Fund organization is most desirable and most necessary in order to deal with the special cases that continually arise in regard to dependents left by soldiers who have gone to the front, it is not right or reasonable that these dependents should have to depend upon public subscriptions for any part of that amount which is recognized to be a necessary allowance for their support. When the war broke out, of course, everything was done hurriedly, and it can easily be understood that every condition could not be adjusted at that particular time. But time has gone on, it is a year and a half now since the war broke out, conditions have developed that possibly were not expected to develop at the time and it is found that the Patriotic Fund is called upon to pay a fixed amount, forming part of the necessary allowance for the family and dependents of a soldier, over and above the extraordinary circumstances which frequently arise and which naturally would be dealt with by such an organization as the Patriotic Fund. I find that in eastern Canada there is a stated allowance from the Patriotic Fund to the dependents of a soldier of $5. In the western provinces the amount is very much larger. I maintain that when, by experience, it has been demonstrated that a soldier's family requires an amount over and above the separation allowance and the assigned pay, that man's separation allowance should be increased to that amount and the Patriotic Fund should not be called upon to meet that requirement. Until conditions had developed and become adjusted, the Patriotic Fund was created for the purpose of filling the gap between the Government provision and the requirements of dependents, but now that these requirements have come to be recognized as established, I see every reason why the Government's separation allowance should be increased so as to relieve the Patriotic Fund from that permanent liability, so to speak, which is such a tremendous call upon the patriotism and benevolence of the people of the country.
It has been said by the gentleman who so ably manages the Patriotic Fund that this fund is necessary to intervene between the requirements of depenedents and the arrangements of the Government because conditions differ in different provinces, and because the Government could not make an arrangement whereby the separa- [DOT] tion allowance would be different in one

province from what it is in another. That argument was perfectly good at the outbreak of hostilities when conditions were new, but now that conditions have become settled and adjusted, it is absolutely established that in British Columbia the family of a soldier require a certain fixed amount to give them a decent living, while in Prince Edward Island a certain les3 amount is required. The facts are now thoroughly understood from one end of the Dominion to the other, and I maintain that the time has arrived when the Patriotic Fund should be relieved from that burden which it now carries and which is properly a part of the burden to be carried by the nation at large. I recall having heard the gentleman who is at the head of the Patriotic Fund suggest, as another reason for the existence of this fund, that it gave an opportunity to those who were not able to render personal service to do service by the contribution of their wealth, their earnings or their savings as the case might be. That is. a perfectly good position to take providing it is not pushed too far. But I submit that when the people of a patriotic, liberal and benevolent disposition are called upon to supply a fixed requirement that properly rests upon the nation at large, it is not a fair proposition and that requirement should not be continued. As long as the burden was light it mattered comparatively little which way it was carried. Now, the burden has become very great upon .the people who are liberal minded and who have responded, I may 6ay, magnificently to the demands that have been made upon them up to the present time. These demands are still increasing, and must necessarily increase. It is not fair that, because certain of our citizens are liberal minded, patriotic and benevolent, that section of the community should carry this burden on their shoulders when it is a burden that properly rests upon the shoulders of every citizen of the country and should be shared in equally by those citizens according to their tax-paying power.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman suggesting that the Patriotic Fund should come to an end?
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I gather that
from what my hon. friend has said.'
Mr. OLIVER < No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He suggests that the burden be placed upon the public?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If I understand him correctly he asks that the burden, as carried by the Patriotic Fund, should cease.

No, that part of it, that is a fixed and stated amount, should be borne by the state and not by private subscription. When it becomes a fixed fact, that in the province of Ontario, we will say, instead of a dependent wife being able to get along with $20 separation allowance and $15 assigned pay, she requires in addition $5 from the Patriotic Fund, the state should assume the burden of providing that $5 and the Patriotic Fund should not be called upon to meet that requirement. The idea that is present in my mind as to the proper function of the Patriotic Fund is to take care of extraordinary conditions which always arise and which no Government could possibly take care of. That is the proper purpose of it, as I would understand it. But it certainly is not proper that this fund, depending on public subscriptions, and levied on a part of the people, should be depended upon to meet those requirements which are stated and fixed requirements, thoroughly well understood, and which certainly should be borne by the state as a whole, by which means every citizen has a share in the burden and responsibility.
Would you increase the separation allowance?
Yes.
Under the Patriotic Fund people do not receive the same amounts in different provinces.
No.
Then how could the Government arrange that they could give people in one province a certain separation allowance and in another province another separation allowance? They could do that, could they?

Yes. After the declaration of war, when nothing was adjusted, when conditions had not settled down, there was possibly a very good reason for the use of this fund to the extent to which it is at present used, and that reason I have heard stated by the president of the fund, but that condition does not exist to-day. It is settled now that in British Columbia a

family requires a minimum amount, a part of which is noiw provided by the Patriotic Fund. There is no reason why the Patriotic Fund should be called upon to supplement the present allowance in order that the minimum amount may be allowed. There is no reason why the Government should not provide a proper amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I understand my hon.
friend to argue that the amount dependents of soldiers require for their wants and requirements, over and above the assigned pay, separation allowance and what they may get from the Patriotic Fund, should be supplied by the state. If that is done, what is left for the Patriotic Fund to do?

The .proper purpose of the Patriotic Fund is to take care of special circumstances that may arise, in which the requirements are over and above the ordinary. I need not say, after the discussions my hon. friend and I have had on recent occasions, that these special oases come up by the hundred, and there is every reason for a Patriotic Fund for the benefit of these dependents. Rut apart from that, it is thoroughly understood that a certain fixed requirement exists in British Columbia, for instance, and a certain fixed requirement in Ontario, and Prince Edward Island, and so on, and I say that public benevolence and patriotism should not be called' on to meet that requirement. It is a fixed requirement and should be met out of the public treasury. It is not fair, either to the soldier or his dependents, or the Service, or to the state, that the present condition of affairs (should continue. Let me point out in this connection that it is recognized in many places throughout the country that the money is not collected on a fair basis. A county council will say: We will contribute so much to the Patriotic Fund, and will then proceed to raise the. amount by taxation. This is done fo.y municipal and county councils throughout the Dominion; they meet their contributions to the Patriotic Fund by levying a tax. I maintain that the time has come when the state at large should leviy the necessary taxation to meet those requirements, instead of calling upon the benevolence and patriotism of the people. That is the view I desire to bring before the House, and desire to bring it forward very strongly for this reason. As the demands increase and they must increase -I fear that the next call for subscriptions

to the Patriotic Fund will not meet with the same generous response that has been met with in the past; and Certainly we cannot afford to allow the dependents of our soldiers to fail to receive that- contribution that was the expectation of the soldier when he enlisted. When the soldier enlisted he expected his family to receive certain assistance: separation allowance, assigned pay, and a certain fixed amount from the Patriotic Fund. While that was not a legal and a binding bargain I maintain that this country is bound in honour to see that every dollar of that money is paid, and that the allowance is kept up to what the soldier when he enlisted, understood his dependents would receive. ' I am sorry to say that during the past months, for reasons said to be good- and very likely good, because it was believed the Patriotic Fund was not able to stand the strain that was being put upon it-there have been certain readjustments and a certain scaling down of the allowance paid to the families of soldiers at the front. I need hardly say that a case of that kind leaves a very unfavourable impression; it is unfortunate that cases of that kind should ever occur, but they do occur, and it certainly is not for the good of the cause that they should occur. I maintain that the State should fully discharge its obligation in respect of the dependents of soldiers at the front and that the Patriotic Fund should take care of extraordinary conditions that may arise in regard to those dependents; in that respect, it has a responsibility, and that is the only responsibility the country at large should expect it to fulfil.
There is another matter that I feel to be so very important and so very serious that I cannot allow it to go by without noticing it. I have had occasion when the Estimates of the Department of Militia have been up to consider the arming of the troops both as to rifles and machine guns. The Prime Minister said that a report had been made in regard to the Ross rifle, with which the Canadian troops are armed. I asked if that report could be made public, and he said no. The only conclusion I can reach is this: That if the report had been favourable it could and would have been made public. But from the fact that it is not considered sound policy to make it public, the only conclusion to be drawn is that the report could not have been considered favourable. I appreciate very deeply the responsibility I take, but I ap-

preciate also the responsibility that rests upon a representative of the Canadian people in this House-a responsibility that demands that no effort shall be left undone to secure to the highest possible degree the efficiency of our troops, and particularly the efficiency of the -weapons with which they are armed.
The Ottawa Citizen of this morning publishes what purports to be extracts from a letter from Gen. Alderson, who is spoken of as Commander-inJChief of the Canadian forces at the front, and the letter is said to be in reply to a communication from Ottawa on the subject.
Who is it addressed to, and what is the date of it?

I could not say. The paper does not give the date. This responsible journal, published in the capital of Canada, publishes what purports to be extracts from a letter which it tacitly represents to be ail official letter from General Alderson, recently commanding the Canadian forces in France. I cannot imagine any Government allowing such statements to appear in the public press for one hour without taking steps to contradict them, if they are susceptible of contradiction.
I read an extract from what purports to be a letter from General Alderson. The suggestion of the newspaper in which it appears is that it is an official letter:
I may say that "very soon after we got out here with the First Division," says General Alderson, "I found that the men were picking up the Lee-Enfields whenever they could and throwing away the Rosses. I issued an order that this was not to be allowed, and prior to the second battle of Ypres that order was carried out. The experience of the battle showed that the Ross jammed so badly that I was obliged to let this order die a natural death. When the division was re-armed with the Lee-Enfield the men cheered loudly on hearing the news, and it was found that there were already more than 3,000 of the rifles in the division.
I hold no brief for the Lee-Enfield, and I did, and still do as regards the 2nd and 3rd Divisions, discourage any crying down of the Ross, although I know, as does every one else, that the Lee-Enfield is out and opt the best active service rifle.
I believe the Ross to be a closer shooting rifle and I think, and I often say so, that with teams of equal shots on the range and using the rifles as single loaders the Ross would win.
General Alderson then refers to a statement that, with three certain marks of ammunition, which he names, the Lee-Enfield "cannot be relied upon to Are fifteen rounds."
"This is absolute invention," he declares. "I attach a copy of a report on the test of ammunition we had when Carson and Max Aitken were last here together. From this you will see that the Lee-Enfield fired from 100 to 125
rounds, as rapidly as possible, with all three marks of ammunition named, while the Ross jammed from the 25th to the 50th round.
" This report, which as you will see was signed by both Carson and Aitken, does not state, as it should, that the Lee-Enfield, although handled by men not trained to it, fired (owing to it being much easier to charge the magazines) its 100 rounds in about one-third less time than the Ross. Nor does the report state, as was the case, that the hands of the men using the Ross were cut and bleeding owing to the difficulty they had in knocking back the bolts.
"None of thpse present, and there were many commanding and other officers there, could have failed to notice these important points."
General Alderson then refers to a statement by a writer of a certain letter that the classes of ammunition in question have "again in some mysterious way" found their way to the Canadian trenches. "That, too, is against the Ross," General Alderson continues. "Moreover, it emphasises what we have been told officially, viz., that while we are stationary it will be possible to keep this ammunition away from the units armed with the Ross, but that when we get on the move it may not be possible."

What ammunition is
that?

I could not say. It is ammunition that is complained about in some, way. I am sorry that the Prime Minister was not in his place when I brought this matter up, but the item was under discussion ano I was compelled to deal with it now or not at all. I am glad to see the-right hon. gentleman now in his place. I have stated that I appreciate the very serious character of this statement, but it appears in a newspaper published in the capital, and I cannot conceive that such a report would be allowed to have publicity for an hour without being specifically contradicted if it could be contradicted.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend might have been better advised to submit the matter to some member of the Government, and perhaps to myself, before bringing it up in the House. The statement that has appeared in the press was brought to the attention of the Government this morning, and, after consultation with my colleagues, I have already taken certain action with regard to it. I desire to say, in the first place, that even if the Ross rifle were the best rifle in the world it would be possible to destroy its usefulness by making and circulating public statements oi that character about it; and it is far from a patriotic service to discredit the only rifle which we are capable of producing in Canada at present. No one is more convinced of the absolute necessity that our

men fighting in the trenches shall be armed with an efficient and effective weapon than the members of the Government, in common with all good .citizens. As I stated in a debate in this House during the present session, there has been criticism of the Koas rifle. There has also, I believe, been criticism of the Lee-Enfield rifle. I repeat what I have already stated on that subject, that probably each of these rifles may have some special advantages over the other.
So far as I am aware, no such letter as that which appeared in the Citizen of this morning has come to the attention of the Government. However, I shall make further inquiry before eight o'clock to ascertain the facts. Diligent inquiry as to the existence of such a letter will be made, and the subject is already under investigation. Even if such a letter were written, it is my judgment that its publication without any communication with the Government, without any inquiry as to the existing situation is not a patriotic service tc this country at this time. I am not alluding to my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver); he has taken it from the public press, but his action does, of course, give it greater publicity than it otherwise would have had.
I desire, further, to announce this-within the past week a communication has been sent to the Commander-in-Chief ax the front, desiring him, on his own behalf, and for the information of the Government of Canada, to make a thorough test of the Ross rifle under precisely the same conditions as those under which that rifle is ordinarily used by our men at the front, and to make also a corresponding test and investigation of the Lee-Enfield rifle. I have no reason to believe that there will be any lack of effective action by Sir Douglas Haig in making that test and investigation^. When, it has been made, it will be for the Government and for the mili-. tary advisers of the Government to consider whether and to what extent it should be made public. It is desirable in view of all these allegations that such a test and investigation should be made; and I felt it my duty after careful consultation with the Minister of Militia and Defence during the past week to request that that course should be taken.
I repeat that we are making inquiry into the reasons which led to the publication of this alleged letter in the press and of the source from which it emanated. We shall take such action in regard thereto as may

seem proper and appropriate under the circumstances and in the interest of the people, especially in the interest of the gallant men tvho are using this rifle at the front.

I understand that the
Prime Minister will give some information to the committee at eight o'clock?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.
Will there be an opportunity then to say something in regard to it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

It seems to me that the hon. member for Edmonton should not be found fault with for bringing this very important matter to the attention of the committee. It must be borne.in mind that this letter purports to be a letter from the gentleman who has been commanding the Canadian forces at the front and who is, I understand, in charge of the Canadian expeditionary forces in Great Britain.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
He is not ip
charge of them.

He has been in charge
of the Canadian forces -.at the front.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He has been in charge of the Canadian forces at the front, and the post which has been suggested-I do not know whether he occupies it as yet -is that of Inspector General of the Canadian forces in Great Britain.

We can hardly believe
that the Citizen would publish a letter of such great importance unless they were satisfied that it was a genuine letter from General Alderson. It bears on its face evidence of its being a reply to some one who had the right to communicate with General Alderson with regard to the Ross rifle. I would assume that it is in reply to a letter which has been sent to him by the Minister of Militia. It bears evidence of that on its face, because it is evidently written in reply to some one who has been defending the Ross rifle. Besides, the familiarity with which General Alderson refers to Mr. Carson and Sir Max Aitken shows that it is written to one with whom his relations have been intimate from a military standpoint. I suggest to my right hon. friend that he should, in connection with the inquiries which he makes, endeavour to ascertain whether a letter was written by the Minister of Militia to General Alderson, and whether or not this letter is in reply. This is a subject in which the House and 1
MAY 17, 101b
the people take a very deep interest, and it would be well that full information should be afforded in reference to the matter. It is desirable that any question with regard to the arms which are supplied to our boys at the front should be settled in satisfactory manner. Every one will agree that no equipment should be furnished to them except it be of the very highest character. There is one very singular remark which is made in the letter, in reference to ammunition. I would judge from the statement of General Alderson that in some inexplicable manner ammunition 'has been supplied to the soldiers which ought not to have been supplied to them. This is a matter which ought to be inquired into and with regard to which the House and the country are entitled to information. There is certainly no very great harm in bringing these matters before the committee for the purpose of having any mystery in regard to them cleared up, as compared with the injury which might result through defective ammunition or arms being supplied to Canadian soldiers at the front. I think the hon. member for Edmonton has performed a very important duty in bringing the matter to the attention of the committee.

I wish to suggest an amendment to the resolution now before the committee with a view to correcting a clerical error. I move that the word "Randolph" be substituted for the word "Robert" in the item providing for a compassionate allowance to the late Mr. Fanning. The name should be Randolph Fanning.

I have been requested by the widow of the late Mr. Laplante to ask the Government whether something better could not have been done for her.
I think that Mrs. Laplante was deserving of a little more consideration on the part of the Government. Was the matter discussed with members of the family?

I do not know that.
Mr. CASGRA1N: We took pains to get information and to consider very carefully ' all the circumstances surrounding the condition in which Mrs. Laplante was left. A less amount was at first suggested, but after investigating the matter we came to the conclusion that $5,000 would be a reasonable amount to pay. I think that my hon. friend will come to the same conclusion

I am speaking from hearsay. I was told that the family of Mr. Laplante lost in the fire some very valuable papers which, if edited as they were intended to be edited by him, would have given his family quite a revenue. That is the reason I bring this matter to the attention of the Government. Of course, if it has been thoroughly investigated I have nothing more to say.
Amendment of Mr. Rogers agreed to.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at eight o'clock, Mr. Rhodes in the Chair.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I find that the communication to Sir Douglas Haig, the Commander in Chief, to which I alluded was not sent as long ago as I thought. It was sent about three days ago. It stated that, in consequence of some criticism which had arisen, the Canadian Government were prepared to leave all questions as to the Ross rifle to the judgment of the Commander in Chief after he had made all necessary tests made under such conditions as are experienced at the front. That is the situation to-day.
Air. OLIVER ' Was that a cablegram?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That was a cablegram, yes. As to the letter which has been published in the press, I communicated with General Hughes, who told me that he had received no such letter, and that there is no official letter of that character. That is all the information I can give to the committee about it.

The letter is of such a
character, the statements contained in it are so serious, that I should think the Government would be very well warranted in pushing inquiry as to how such statements came to be published under the presumed authority under which they were published. We have a censorship in Canada, and if this letter is not a bona fide letter of General Alderson's, it certainly ought to come within the range of the activity of the censor.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Inquiry was
made by the Solicitor General, whom I asked to take up the subject with the censor. The censor informed him that he had no knowledge of the proposed publication or of the letter, and that the first intimation he had of it was the appearance of this alleged communication in the press

We do not propose to drop the matter without further inquiry.

Without making any
disparaging statements, I may call attention to the fact that last year I read to the Minister of Militia a letter which was published in the Canadian Courier, signed by one of our boys at the front, in which he stated that the first thing they did when Ih^y left the camp in England for France was to discard the Eoss rifle.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
And I might
say that possibly some incidents of that kind may have taken place to which not too much importance should be attached.
I believe that a good deal of the equipment which the First Canadian Division took over was left on Salisbury Plain when the troops went to the front.
A Board of Inquiry was called by the representatives of the Canadian Government on the other side for the purpose of determining whether that equipment was inefficient for use. As a result of that inquiry it was declared to be perfectly good equipment, although in some respects not precisely of the same character as that adopted in Great Britain. Thus the people nf this country got credit for that equipment which was taken over, after being declared perfectly efficient for the purpose for which it was designed.
I questioned all the boys who came back from the front to our town about this, and they all agreed that the Ross rifle was perfectly all right.

The statements before the House are undoubtedly very serious. They have a deep meaning and must be of deep interest to a great .many people in the country. I rather regard the statements that have been made, such as that of the hon. member for Rouville of a moment ago, which I am sure 'he really did not intend [DOT] to make-

I was simply recalling the fact that these attacks against the Ross rifle are not new. Last year, just for the .purpose of inquiry, I read to the Minister of Militia a letter published in the Canadian Courier, signed by one of the boys at the front, in which he stated, inter alia, in giving news about the departure for France and that sort of thing, that one of the first things they did was to discard the Ross rifle. I am not passing judgment on the Ross rifle. I am well aware that there are several competitors for the

supply of weapons in time of war, and it might be quite possible that it is the policy of certain people to play an unfair game as against the Ross rifle. I am not passing judgment, but I am saying that it is not at all a new accusation.

I appreciate what my
hon. friend has just said. It is certainly not a new accusation, and the letter that ,ha6 been quoted, if we are to understand it at all, is not new either, although it has been published without any date and without the address of the person to whom it was sent. But the letter seems to leave an impression that there is something very .seriously wrong, although a correct reading of the letter, with a knowledge of the circumstances, would not bear out that impression. We have already had information that when our men went over at first, in the using, of the different series of ammunition with which they were supplied, (a certain amount of jamming took place in the Ross rifle it is said and also in the Lee-Enfield rifle. That is information which I believe to be correct, and which we have bad; and if this letter was written of that-date, why then, of course, it is a thing of the past. The conditions complained of at that time have been remedied. The chamber of the Ross rifle has been enlarged in such a manner that the difficulties that were met with a year ago or more have been corrected. So far as I know, with any information it has been possible for me to obtain, there has been no difficulty and no jamming of the Ross rifle for many months past, especially since .the chambers were corrected to receive almost any series of ammunition that might be supplied. It is true that in the early days, before they had the war ammunitions running as correctly as they are to-day, certain difficulties arose, and it seems unfortunate that we should have this letter published without any date, with a view, evidently, of trying to create a very false impression and to create a feeling of unrest in the minds of the mothers, and the sisters and the wives of the bravest and the best of our sons, who are now doing duty on the firing line, fighting for us. It is most unfortunate that there should be published such a letter as that which appears in ,the Citizen newspaper of the city of Ottawa. I am not surprised that that paper would be guilty of publishing this letter, or anything else by which they could hope to create^excite-ment.'

I should like to read a letter or two from gentlemen who have a knowledge of the facts, in order that we may, if we possibly can, correct the false impression that has been created by the publication of this letter, because I say that, so far as I can ascertain, this letter is not an official letter. I know from the statement of my friend the Prime Minister that it has not been received by him, and I know from the Minister of Militia that it has not been addressed to him. Therefore, if such a letter is in existence, the individual, if he is an employee of the Government or if he is a member of the staff, or if he holds any other position in this country, who would be guilty of publishing this letter in the mysterious form in which it is published -the proper place for him would be in the tower of this building; and so far as I am concerned, I should be glad to be a party to placing him there.
But the tower is down.

I will promise my hon. friend to provide a suitable tower for the individual who wrote that letter if we can locate him, and we will take good care of him, too. Allow me to read the following letter dated London, 14th April, 1916:
Sir,-It will be of interest to you to know that Lieutenant Ross, 17th Battalion, in practice this afternoon fired 145 rounds in 7 minutes. I believe a speed of 160 rounds is attainable. Best rate claimed by Hythe Staff with Enfield is, 121 rounds.
In one minute test Ross rifles averaged 21 rounds (nearly) against 17 (nearly) for Enfield, Expect to see Ross record improved, but not Enfield.
An interesting test was made with eight firers. Four men trained with Enfields were given Ross rifles. Four Ross men were given Enfields. As might have been expected Ross men did not do well with Enfield, but the remarkable thing was that all Enfield men without training, exceeded or equalled best previous records with Enfield. Detailed records will be sent you shortly.
Respectfully,
(Sgd.) Roy B. Gibson. Major-General Sir Sam Hughes.
I read this report from Capt. C. H. Ackerman to the Minister of Militia:
Kingston, Ontario, 18th January, 1916. From,-Captain C. H. Ackerman,
2nd Battalion Canadians,
To,-Major-General Sir Sam Hughes,
Minister of Miltia and Defence, Ottawa, Ont.
Report on Ross rifle.
Sir,-I have the honour to report on my experiences in the trenches with the Ross rifle.
The Ross rifle used by the First Canadian division in France was exchanged for the Lee-
Enfield rifle during the second week in June by the Second Battalion to which I was attached. I myself, used this rifle in the trenches and I felt I did very much more effective work than I could have done with a Lee-Enfield, owing to the improved rear aperture sight of the Ross and the protected block foresight which is covered with a hood and permits of a more uniform light which is essential to good shooting. The rear aperture sight is a decided improvement on the open back sight because the full sighting power of the eye is concentrated on one point through this aperture and this power is, when the rifle is properly sighted, directly in line with the block foresight and the target; this, I consider the one outstanding advantage over the Lee-Enfield rifle. (If it is not conducive to bettor shooting than the Enfield, why did the National Association object to its use at Bisley in 1913).
In the second battle of Ypres, at St. Julien and Langemarck, when we were first called uppn to put the rifle to a severe active service test, we had trouble extracting the shell or in pulling the bolt back after a shot was fired, and I believe other battalions experienced the same difficulty. After our battalion came out to rest I had occasion to test, under orders, from my commanding officer, all the rifles in my company that had given trouble. In my test I discovered the Canadian ammunition to work perfectly and some series of British worked comparatively well, but the most of the British ammunition caused the bolt to stick after each shot was fired. Even without firing the same difficulty was experienced, so that proved conclusively that the various series of ammunition used were not uniform, shortly afterwards the rifles were all taken from the First Canadian division and the chambers were slightly enlarged .459" to .464" at the base, overcoming the difficulty of having the bolt drag during the extraction of the shell.
I, myself, left the trenches wounded in June and was unable to observe personally the results of the enlarging of the chamber, but have inquired since coming home and I find that difficulty has been overcome and now I consider the Ross rifle the most perfect of the four rifles that I had the opportunity of trying, viz., Mauser (German with no protection for foresight and with open back sight.) Lebel (French with same sighting apparatus) and Lee-Enfield (British with partially protected foresight).
I have heard it said that the aperture back sight of the Ross rifle was too frail, but in more than four months of trench warfare, I had trouble with no more than three sights in my platoon of 55 men. This trouble was caused by permitting the rifle to fall against some hard body with the leaf raised; this same trouble might easily.happen to an Enfield.
When our men first saw the Lee-Enfield what appealed to them most was the magazine which held two charges or ten pounds of ammunition. This, at first, appeared to be an advantage, but actually it resulted in a greater waste of ammunition than was experienced with the Ross. It must be remembered that in actual trench warfare, many hundreds of thousands of rounds of ammunition are fired from rifles and wasted, owing to the lack of a suitable target and when the difficulty of bringing in ammunition under fire is taken into consideration, the man with a ten round magazine is bound to fire off his whole magazine of ten in all probability waste all ten.
'Tis true that in case of a German attack on our trenches, a man has more confidence in a



rifle when he knows he has ten rounds ready to fire without unloading, hut in my own experience, I found that the responsibility of breaking up a German attack on our trenches very seldom rested on the fire of our rifles. It rested on the support of our artillery, machine guns, bombs and the usual defensive works in front of the trenches such as ditches, wire entanglements, etc.
The above report is a true statement r of my own experience with the Canadian service rifle and I feel that personally I would want no better rifle to go into action with again.
I have the honour to be, sir,
Your obedient servant,
(Sgd.) C. H. Ackerman,
Captain,
2nd Battalion Canadians.
Here is another letter from J. C. Mac-dougall, Shorncliffe:
With reference to the minister's cable of the 14th instant regarding the jamming of the Lee-Enfield and Ross rifles when using bad ammunition.
No cases of jamming of either rifles have occurred here for months, and the confidence of the men in both weapons and ammunition has been established. Both rifles jammed in the past when using B.14 and G.14 and certain Marks of D.C. ammunition. The steps then taken were to withdraw the bad ammunition.
I desire to read, also, a report from a gentleman whose name will be received with respect, not only by the members of this House, but by the people of Canada at large, in respect to this important matter. I am troubling the House with the view of putting this on record so that there may be no feeling of unrest among the people of Canada, who have such a deep interest in the welfare of our soldiers at t'he front. This letter is dated Headquarters, Shorncliffe, 26th April, 1916, and is addressed to Sir Sam Hughes:
Re DEMONSTRATION OP RAPID FIRE Ross and Lee-Enfield Rifles.
I enclose you herewith a report (which has just reached me) of a demonstration of rapid fire with both the Ross and Lee-Enfield rifles which was carried out on the Hythe Ranges on the 8th April, 1916, together with statements showing results, and from which it will be seen that the Ross rifle is a superior small arm to the Lee-Enfield, capable of developing a higher rate of fire, whilst still maintaining its accuracy.
With kindest regards,
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd.) S. B. STEELE,
Major-General.
The report which General Steele transmits for the'information of the department, and for the information of the people of Canada, is as follows:

Musketry Office,
Headquarters,
Canadian Training Division, Shorncliffe,
11th April, 1916.
From: Lieut.-Colonel E. Frismall,
Att'd. G.S. (Musketry).
To:	The General Officer Commanding,
Canadian Training Division.
Sir,

I have the honour to report:-
A demonstration of rapid fire with both Ross and S.M. Lee-Enfield rifles was carried out on "A" Range, Hythe, at 2.30 p.m. 8th April, 1916. Officers present.
Major-General S. B. Steele, G.O.C. Troops, Shorncliffe.
Brig.-General Landry, G.O.C. 11th C.R.I.B.
Lieut.-Col. Ashton, O.C. 12th C.R.I.B.
Lieut.-Col. Cowan, O.C. 13th C.R.I.B.
Lieut.-Col. Prismall, Musketry Staff Officer, and other officers from the Divisional and Brigade Staffs and Battalions of the Canadian Training Division.
Executive Officer, Lieut. A. Raker.
The demonstration was divided into two parts. In the first part a number of men fired as many rounds in one minute as they were able.
In the second part two firers, one with the Ross rifle and the other with the S.M. Lee-Enfield fired for seven consecutive minutes as many rounds as they were able.
The results, which are attached, show that a high rate of fire can be reached by trained firers. Constant practice in loading and handling the rifle, however, is necessary if a high standard of efficiency is to be reached and maintained.
The seven-minute continuous fire illustrated practically the limitations of rapid Are and the effect on both rifle and firer. The fatigue of the firers. the heating of the barrel and conse-' quent difficulty in aiming were apparent.
Both rifles worked well, extraction was good, and the bolts worked smoothly.	.
The ammunition used was D.A. 1915.
After this demonstration was concluded, a series of shots with defective ammunition (B. 14) was fired, and greater trouble was experienced in extraction with the Lee-Enfield than the Ross rifle.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
(Sgd.) E. PRISMALL,
Lieut.-Colonel, Att'd. G.S. (Musketry) Can. Training Division.
Attached to this letter is a table showing t'he number of shots fired 'by each individual and giving the names of the men in the test. I will give it to Hansard, so that it will go out to the country and satisfy the people that we have the good fortune to possess a rifle that takes second place probably to none at the present time. It will reassure them that it is not the misfortune of our soldiers to suffer from the effects of a bad rifle. It is true that in the earlier stages of the war they did suffer from the effects of bad ammunition, but that

defect has been corrected. I repeat that it is most unfortunate that any 'uneasiness should 'be caused by the publication of the letter which has been referred to, and which is probably of old date and intended simply to create uneasiness and unrest. It is most unfortunate in t'he interests of the country, and in every other way, and it is only fair, and, indeed, the duty, of the
hon. members of this House to correct any such impression, and to assist in punishing, if possible, the individual, whoever he may be, who was guilty of committing such an offence as to publish a letter without the proper heading, without date, and containing information that is not correct.
